catalog_quote: The stress is not distinctive in Bhujel. All the monosyllabic lexical words such as nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs and verbs are always stressed, as shown in (39) ... A great majority of the disyllabic nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs and verbs infinitives receive stress on the second syllable from the last i.e penultimate syllable, e.g. (40) a. /ˈanyʌ/ 'elder sister' ... e. /ˈkʌymay/ 'to quarrel' f. /ˈkʌtʰure/ 'young' There are a number of disyllabic words which receive the stress in the ultimate syllable, as in (41) a. /saˈwat/ 'echo' ... In Bhujel the verbs inflected with a causative morpheme -tʌk get stress in the penultimate syllable, e.g., (42) ... b. /nʰi-ˈtak-ʌl/ 'caused to laugh' Bhujel has borrowed a large amount of Nepali vocabulary. They have been accommodated to Nepali stress pattern. [5.2.1] Normally there has been observed stress in the first syllable in Bhujel. However, the stress has been found shifted to the second syllable in the phonological words. It can be formalized as follows: (60) ˈCV(C) CV(C) → CV(C) ˈCV(C)CV(C) ... (61) a. [ˈje-ʌl] eat-PST [je-ˈlʌk-ʌl] eat-COMPL-PST ... c. [ˈpukʰ-ge-ʌl] head-be-PST [pu-ˈge-ʌl] head-be-PST ... f. [ˈbay-n-u-ŋ] Give-NPST-DIR-1/2 [bay-ˈce-n-u-ŋ] give-CERT-NPST-DIR-1/2 [3.6] The stress is weak in Bhujel. It is mainly on the root of the word. Unlike Chepang and Kham, Bhujel lacks tone. [ch. 13] The stress is placed on the root at the word boundary position in Bhujel (see 3.5.1 for details).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and weak. Monosyllabic lexical words are stressed; disyllabic words (mostly root + suffix) are overwhelmingly stressed on the first = penultimate syllable; when a further suffix makes the word trisyllabic the stress moves to the second syllable, which in every example given (e.g. eat-COMPL-PST, die-PERF-PST, stay-PTCP-NPST) is again the penult; causatives in -tak are penult-stressed. A lexically listed set of disyllables ('echo', 'shin', 'mosquito', 'bamboo shoot', 'tear', 'after that', 'by whom') has final stress, and Nepali loans keep Nepali stress. The author himself summarises the system as 'weak stress, mainly on the root, word-boundary' (ch.3 summary, ch.13 typology table), which fits the disyllables but not his trisyllabic stress-shift data; the surface generalisation that covers both is penultimate. No acoustic evidence; impressionistic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no secondary stress marked or mentioned).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) 'a number of disyllabic words' with ultimate stress, listed lexically (ex. 41: 'echo', 'shin', 'by whom', 'mosquito', 'bamboo shoot', 'tear', 'after that'); (ii) Nepali loanwords 'accommodated to Nepali stress pattern'; (iii) compounds are treated as a single word for stress (ch.6, p.~176). Author's alternative framing: stress 'mainly on the root' / 'normally in the first syllable', shifting to the second syllable in longer inflected words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms and inflected verb words ('phonological words'); sentence-level 'tonic stress' on the verb / focused constituent is treated separately under intonation (sec. 3.5.2, ch.10). Language explicitly described as non-tonal ('Unlike Chepang and Kham, Bhujel lacks tone'). IPA in the PDF is rendered in Symbol/Greek glyphs (legacy SIL font substitution), so example transcriptions are only partly legible; the prose is intact.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Bhujel (autonym 'Bhujel talk'), glottocode bujh1238 / ISO byh, as spoken along the Mahabharat range of Tanahun District, Nepal (west of the Narayani); Glottolog's name 'Bujhyal' and Caughley's 'Bujheli' (formerly treated as a dialect of Chepang, chep1245, speakers formerly called Gharti) refer to the same variety. No dialect split is described; the thesis treats the Tanahun speech as a single form.
